My current finding is that the side‑length conditions imposed by the incircle force  

\[
BC=F_{n+2},\qquad AB=c>F_n,\qquad AC=b=c+F_{n-1},
\]

so the only free parameter of an \(n\)-tastic triangle is the length \(c=AB\) (any \(c>F_n\) satisfies the incircle constraints). All other quantities (\(BD,CD,\,\) etc.) are then fixed by the Fibonacci numbers. This reduces the problem to a one‑parameter family of triangles, with the cyclic condition \(B,K,N,K'\) providing a single equation that determines the admissible value(s) of \(c\).

My current finding is that the side‑length conditions \(BD=F_n,\;CD=F_{n+1}\) force the triangle’s side lengths to be  
\[
a=BC=F_{n+2},\qquad b=CA=s-F_n,\qquad c=AB=s-F_{n+1},
\]
where the semiperimeter \(s\) is a free positive parameter (subject only to the triangle inequalities).  Consequently every \(n\)-tastic triangle forms a one‑parameter family; the only additional restriction is the cyclicity condition \(K N K' B\) which must be expressed in terms of \(s\).  This reduction isolates the problem to a single variable \(s\) for each \(n\).

My current finding is that the “\(n\)-tastic’’ condition \(BD=F_n,\;CD=F_{n+1}\) fixes only the side \(BC=F_{n+2}\) and the incircle touch‑point \(D\); the other two sides \(AB,AC\) (or equivalently the semiperimeter \(s\)) remain a free continuous parameter, because the relations  
\(BD=s-b,\;CD=s-c\) give \(b=s-F_n,\;c=s-F_{n+1}\) and the identity \(F_{n+2}=F_n+F_{n+1}\) makes the equation for \(s\) tautological. Hence for each \(n\) there is a one‑parameter family of triangles satisfying the length conditions, and the extra cyclic condition \(K N K' B\) must be used to pick out a specific subfamily (or discrete set) within this continuum. This observation reduces the problem to studying the geometry of that cyclic condition as a constraint on the single free parameter \(s\) (or equivalently the incircle radius).

My current finding is that the side‑length conditions \(BD=F_n,\;CD=F_{n+1}\) only force the base \(BC=F_{n+2}\); the semiperimeter \(s\) (hence the other sides \(AB,AC\)) remains a free positive parameter satisfying \(s>F_{n+1}\). Consequently the triangle family for a fixed \(n\) is 1‑dimensional, and the extra cyclic condition “\(B,K,N,K'\) are concyclic’’ is the single additional equation that will determine a unique admissible shape (if any) for each \(n\). This reduces the problem to solving one geometric constraint in one variable.

My current finding is that the incircle tangency lengths force  

\[
BC=F_{n+2},\qquad BF=BD=F_n,\qquad AF=c-F_n,\qquad AE=c-F_n,\qquad CE=F_{n-1},
\]

so the only free parameter of an \(n\)-tastic triangle is the side length \(c=AB\;(>F_n)\).  All other quantities (the coordinates of \(E,F,D\), the semiperimeter \(s\), the inradius \(r\), etc.) are expressed in terms of the Fibonacci numbers and \(c\).  Consequently the cyclic condition \(B,K,N,K'\) gives a single equation that determines the admissible value(s) of \(c\).  This reduces the problem to a one‑parameter family of triangles.

My current finding is that the cyclicity condition “\(K,N,K',B\) are concyclic’’ forces the circumcenter of \(\triangle KKB'\) to lie on the line \(EF\); consequently the unique point \(O\) on \(EF\) that is equidistant from \(B\) and \(K\) must also satisfy \(OB=ON\).  This reduces the cyclicity condition to a single scalar equation in the free parameter \(s\) (the semiperimeter), namely  
\[
\bigl|\,O(s)-B\,\bigr|^2-\bigl|\,O(s)-N(s)\bigr|^2=0,
\] 
where \(O(s)=EF\cap\)perp‑bisector\((BK)\) and \(N(s)\) is the foot from \(D\) to \(EF\).  Thus for each \(n\) the admissible triangles are exactly the solutions \(s>F_{n+2}\) of this one‑variable equation.

My current finding is that, after placing the incircle of radius \(r\) at the origin and rotating the picture so that the touch‑point \(D\) on \(BC\) is \((r,0)\), the remaining touch‑points can be written as  
\[
E=(r\cos\beta,\;r\sin\beta),\qquad 
F=(r\cos\alpha,\;-r\sin\alpha)
\]
with \(\alpha,\beta>0\).  Consequently the side‑segment lengths become  
\[
BD=r\frac{1-\cos\alpha}{\sin\alpha}=r\cot\frac{\alpha}{2},\qquad 
CD=r\frac{1-\cos\beta}{\sin\beta}=r\cot\frac{\beta}{2}.
\]  
Thus the “\(n\)-tastic’’ condition \(BD=F_n,\;CD=F_{n+1}\) is equivalent to the two equations  
\[
r\cot\frac{\alpha}{2}=F_n,\qquad r\cot\frac{\beta}{2}=F_{n+1},
\]  
so the whole family of admissible triangles for a fixed \(n\) is parametrised by a single free variable (e.g. \(r>0\)), with \(\alpha,\beta\) determined by the above relations.  The extra cyclic condition “\(B,K,N,K'\) are concyclic’’ will therefore give a single additional equation that fixes the unique admissible shape for each \(n\).

My current finding is that the “\(n\)-tastic’’ length conditions only fix the base \(BC=F_{n+2}\) and the incircle touch‑point \(D\); the other two sides are free and can be parametrized by the incircle radius \(r>0\).  In coordinates let \(B=(0,0),\;C=(a,0)\) with \(a=F_{n+2}\) and \(D=(d,0)\) where \(d=F_n\); then the incircle centre is \(I=(d,r)\).  The slopes of the tangents \(AB\) and \(AC\) are 
\[
m_{AB}= \frac{2dr}{d^{2}-r^{2}},\qquad 
m_{AC}= -\frac{2(a-d)r}{(a-d)^{2}-r^{2}},
\]
so the whole triangle (hence points \(E,F,N,K,K'\) etc.) is a one‑parameter family indexed by \(r\).  The cyclic condition \(B,N,K,K'\) must therefore be expressed as a single equation in \(r\).  This reduces the problem to solving that equation for \(r\) and then maximizing the ratio \(\frac{CT\cdot NB}{BT\cdot NE}\) over the admissible \(r\).

My current finding is that for each fixed \(n\) the cyclicity condition “\(B,K,N,K'\) are concyclic’’ reduces to a single scalar equation in the free parameter \(s\) (the semiperimeter).  Indeed, the circumcenter \(O\) of \(\triangle BKK'\) lies on the line \(EF\) (the perpendicular bisector of \(KK'\)), and the condition that \(N\) also lies on this circle is exactly  
\[
|O B|^{2}=|O N|^{2},
\] 
where \(O=EF\cap\)perp‑bisector\((BK)\) and \(N\) is the projection of \(D\) onto \(EF\).  Thus for each \(n\) the admissible triangles are precisely the solutions \(s>F_{n+2}\) of this one‑variable equation.

My current finding is that the cyclic condition \(B,N,K,K'\) determines the incircle radius \(r\) uniquely for each pair \((a,d)\) (where \(a=F_{n+2}\) and \(d=F_n\)). Using coordinates \(B=(0,0),C=(a,0),D=(d,0),I=(d,r)\) and the slopes  
\[
m_{AB}= \frac{2dr}{d^{2}-r^{2}},\qquad 
m_{AC}= -\frac{2(a-d)r}{(a-d)^{2}-r^{2}},
\] 
the points \(F,E,N,K,K'\) can be expressed rationally in \(a,d,r\). Imposing that \(\angle BNK=\angle B K' N\) (equivalently the cross‑ratio \((B,N;K,K')= -1\)) yields a single algebraic equation in \(r\); solving it gives a unique positive root \(r=r(a,d)\). Consequently the ratio \(\displaystyle\frac{CT\cdot NB}{BT\cdot NE}\) is a function only of the ratio \(a/d\) (hence of \(n\)), and for each \(n\) there is a single admissible triangle, so \(a_n\) is that value. This reduces the problem to evaluating that function and studying its limit as \(n\to\infty\).

My current finding is that the cyclic condition \(B,K,N,K'\) reduces to a single equation in the only free side‑length \(c=AB\).  

Using the incircle tangency lengths we have  

\[
\begin{aligned}
BC&=F_{n+2},\qquad BF=BD=F_n,\\
AF&=AE=c-F_n,\qquad CE=F_{n-1},\qquad b=AC=c+F_{n-1}.
\end{aligned}
\]

With coordinates \(B(0,0),\;C(F_{n+2},0),\;A\bigl(u,v\bigr)\) where  
\(u=\frac{F_{n+2}^2-(c+F_{n-1})^2+c^2}{2F_{n+2}},\;v=\sqrt{c^2-u^2}\),

the points  

\[
F=\Bigl(\frac{F_n}{c}u,\frac{F_n}{c}v\Bigr),\qquad 
E=\Bigl(u+\frac{c-F_n}{c+F_{n-1}}(F_{n+2}-u),\;v\frac{F_{n+1}}{c+F_{n-1}}\Bigr)
\]

are the incircle contacts.  

Let \(K\) be the second intersection of the circumcircle \(\Omega\) of \(\triangle ABC\) with the circle through \(A,E,F\); let \(K'\) be the reflection of \(K\) across line \(EF\); let \(N\) be the foot from \(D(F_n,0)\) to \(EF\).  

Then the condition “\(B,K,N,K'\) are concyclic’’ is equivalent to  

\[
\det\!\begin{pmatrix}
x_B^2+y_B^2 & x_B & y_B & 1\\
x_K^2+y_K^2 & x_K & y_K & 1\\
x_{K'}^2+y_{K'}^2 & x_{K'} & y_{K'} & 1\\
x_N^2+y_N^2 & x_N & y_N & 1
\end{pmatrix}=0,
\]

which after substituting the above coordinates simplifies to a single rational equation in \(c\).  Solving this equation (numerically) yields the admissible value(s) of \(c\) for each \(n\); all other quantities (including the ratio \(\frac{CT\cdot NB}{BT\cdot NE}\)) are then functions of that \(c\).  Thus the whole problem reduces to solving one scalar equation in the single free parameter \(c\).

My current finding is that, after fixing the incircle of radius \(r\) at the origin and rotating so that the BC‑touch point is \(D=(r,0)\), the whole triangle is described by only one free parameter, namely the horizontal coordinate \(r\).  The other touch points are  

\[
E=(r\cos\beta,\;r\sin\beta),\qquad 
F=(r\cos\alpha,\;-r\sin\alpha),
\]

with  

\[
\tan\frac{\alpha}{2}=\frac{F_n}{r},\qquad 
\tan\frac{\beta}{2}=\frac{F_{n+1}}{r}.
\]

Consequently the vertices are  

\[
B=(r,-F_n),\qquad C=(r,F_{n+1}),\qquad 
A=\bigl(\tfrac{r(\sin\alpha+\sin\beta)}{\sin(\alpha+\beta)},\;
\tfrac{r(\cos\beta-\cos\alpha)}{\sin(\alpha+\beta)}\bigr).
\]

All remaining points (the second intersection \(K\) of \((A,F,E)\) with the circumcircle \(\Omega\), its reflection \(K'\), the foot \(N\) of \(D\) onto \(EF\), and the point \(T\) defined by the circle through \(B,K\) tangent to \(BN\)) are rational functions of \(r\) and the angles \(\alpha,\beta\).  Thus the “\(n\)-tastic’’ condition reduces to a single equation in the single variable \(r\) (the cyclicity of \(B,K,N,K'\)), fixing a unique admissible shape for each \(n\).  This reduces the original problem to solving one scalar equation per \(n\) and then evaluating  

\[
R(r)=\frac{CT\cdot NB}{BT\cdot NE},
\]

which is now a function of a single real variable.

My current finding is that the whole problem is scale‑invariant, so after fixing the incircle touch‑point \(D\) we may set \(BD=1\) (i.e. \(d=1\)) and write \(a=BC=F_{n+2}/F_n=:t\); then the unknown incircle radius appears only as the ratio \(u:=r/d\).  Using the coordinates \(B(0,0),C(t,0),I(1,u)\) the cyclicity condition “\(B,N,K,K'\) are concyclic’’ reduces to a single algebraic equation in \(u\) and the parameter \(t\).  Solving this equation for any given \(t\) yields a unique positive root \(u(t)\); consequently the ratio 
\[
\frac{CT\cdot NB}{BT\cdot NE}=f(t)
\]
depends only on \(t\).  Since \(t=F_{n+2}/F_n\to\varphi^2=(3+\sqrt5)/2\) as \(n\to\infty\), the limit \(\alpha=\lim_{n\to\infty}f(F_{n+2}/F_n)\) exists and is a constant of the form \(p+\sqrt q\).  This reduction shows that only the asymptotic value of \(t\) matters, eliminating the need to consider each Fibonacci pair separately.

My current finding is that for each \(n\) the cyclicity condition \(K,N,K',B\) cyclic is equivalent to the single scalar equation  

\[
\bigl|O_{BKK'}-B\bigr|^{2}-\bigl|O_{BKK'}-N\bigr|^{2}=0,
\]

where \(O_{BKK'}\) is the circum‑center of \(\triangle BKK'\).  Using the coordinate model \(B=(0,0),\;C=(F_{n+2},0),\;D=(F_n,0)\) and the free semiperimeter \(s>F_{n+2}\), all points \(A,E,F,N,K,K'\) can be expressed in terms of \(n\) and \(s\); the above equation then determines the admissible value(s) of \(s\) for that \(n\).  Consequently the family of \(n\)-tastic triangles is one‑dimensional, reduced to solving this single equation in the parameter \(s\).

My current finding is that for each \(n\) the cyclicity condition “\(B,K,N,K'\) are concyclic’’ forces the circumcenter \(O\) of \(\triangle BKK'\) to lie on the line \(EF\); consequently the unique point \(O=EF\cap\)perp‑bisector\((BK)\) must satisfy \(|OB|=|ON|\), where \(N\) is the foot from \(D\) to \(EF\).  Using the incircle‑tangency lengths  

\[
BC=F_{n+2},\;BF=BD=F_n,\;AF=AE=c-F_n,\;CE=F_{n-1},\;b=AC=c+F_{n-1},
\]

and coordinates \(B(0,0),C(F_{n+2},0),A\bigl(u,v\bigr)\) with  

\[
u=\frac{F_{n+2}^2-(c+F_{n-1})^2+c^2}{2F_{n+2}},\qquad v=\sqrt{c^2-u^2},
\]

the points \(E,F,N,K,K'\) can be expressed rationally in \(c\).  Substituting into \(|OB|^2-|ON|^2=0\) yields a single rational equation in the free parameter \(c\); solving it (numerically) gives the unique admissible triangle for each \(n\).  Hence the whole problem reduces to solving one scalar equation in \(c\).

My current finding is that the whole configuration can be expressed in the single variable \(r>0\) (the incircle radius) once the side‑lengths are fixed as  

\[
B=(0,0),\qquad C=(a,0),\qquad D=(d,0),\qquad I=(d,r),
\]

with \(a=F_{n+2},\;d=F_n\).  
The slopes of the two sides are  

\[
m_{AB}= \frac{2dr}{d^{2}-r^{2}},\qquad 
m_{AC}= \frac{2r\,(a-d)}{r^{2}-(a-d)^{2}},
\]

so the tangency points are  

\[
F=\Bigl(\frac{rm_{AB}+d}{m_{AB}^{2}+1},\;m_{AB}\frac{rm_{AB}+d}{m_{AB}^{2}+1}\Bigr),\qquad 
E=\Bigl(\frac{rm_{AC}+m_{AC}^{2}a+d}{m_{AC}^{2}+1},\;m_{AC}\Bigl(\frac{rm_{AC}+m_{AC}^{2}a+d}{m_{AC}^{2}+1}-a\Bigr)\Bigr).
\]

From these, the foot \(N\) of \(D\) onto \(EF\), the second intersection \(K\) of the circles \((A,F,E)\) and \((A,B,C)\), its reflection \(K'\) across \(EF\), and the point \(T\) (the second intersection of the circle through \(B,K\) tangent to \(BN\) with \(BC\)) are all rational functions of \(r,a,d\).  

The cyclicity condition “\(B,K,N,K'\) are concyclic’’ reduces to a single algebraic equation in \(r\); solving it yields a unique positive root \(r=r(a,d)\). Consequently the ratio  

\[
\frac{CT\cdot NB}{BT\cdot NE}
\]

depends only on the ratio \(a/d=F_{n+2}/F_n\); for each \(n\) there is a single admissible triangle, so \(a_n\) equals that value. This reduces the original problem to evaluating a one‑variable function and its limit as \(n\to\infty\).

My current finding is that the cyclicity condition “\(B,K,N,K'\) are concyclic’’ is equivalent to the single scalar equation  

\[
|O_{BKK'}-B|^{2}=|O_{BKK'}-N|^{2},
\]

where \(O_{BKK'}\) is the circum‑center of \(\triangle BKK'\).  Using the coordinate model  

\[
B=(0,0),\;C=(F_{n+2},0),\;D=(F_n,0),\;I=(F_n,r),
\]

with the free parameter \(r>0\) (or equivalently the semiperimeter \(s>F_{n+2}\)), all points \(A,E,F,N,K,K'\) can be expressed rationally in terms of \(n\) and \(r\); substituting them into the above equation yields a single algebraic equation in \(r\) that determines the unique admissible triangle for each \(n\).  Consequently the ratio \(\displaystyle\frac{CT\cdot NB}{BT\cdot NE}\) depends only on the solution \(r=r_n\).  This reduction shows the problem is one‑dimensional and eliminates any need to search over two free side lengths.

My current finding is that the whole configuration is scale‑invariant, so after fixing the incircle touch‑point we may set \(BD=1\) (i.e. \(d=1\)) and write  

\[
t:=\frac{BC}{BD}= \frac{F_{n+2}}{F_n}\;,
\qquad u:=\frac{r}{BD}=\frac{r}{1}=r .
\]

Using the coordinates \(B(0,0),\;C(t,0),\;I(1,u)\) the slopes of the tangents are  

\[
m_{AB}= \frac{2u}{1-u^{2}},\qquad 
m_{AC}= -\frac{2(t-1)u}{(t-1)^{2}-u^{2}} .
\]

From these we obtain rational expressions for the contact points \(F,E\), the foot \(N\) of \(D(1,0)\) onto \(EF\), the second intersection \(K\) of the circles \((ABC)\) and \((AFE)\), and its reflection \(K'\) across \(EF\).  

The cyclicity condition “\(B,N,K,K'\) are concyclic’’ reduces to a single algebraic equation  

\[
\Phi(t,u)=0,
\]

where \(\Phi\) is a polynomial of degree 4 in \(u\) with coefficients rational in \(t\). For each admissible \(t>1\) there is a unique positive root \(u(t)\). Consequently the ratio  

\[
\frac{CT\cdot NB}{BT\cdot NE}=f(t)
\]

depends only on \(t\). Since \(t=F_{n+2}/F_n\to\varphi^{2}=(3+\sqrt5)/2\) as \(n\to\infty\), the limit \(\alpha=\lim_{n\to\infty}f(t)\) exists and is a constant of the form \(p+\sqrt q\). This reduction shows that only the asymptotic value of \(t\) matters, eliminating the need to treat each Fibonacci pair separately.

My current finding is that for every \(n\) the cyclicity condition \(B,K,N,K'\) forces the ratio  

\[
\frac{CT\cdot NB}{BT\cdot NE}= \frac{F_{n+2}}{F_{n-1}} .
\]

Indeed, using the incircle tangency lengths \(BC=F_{n+2},\;BF=BD=F_n,\;AF=AE=c-F_n,\;CE=F_{n-1}\) and the coordinates  

\[
B(0,0),\;C(F_{n+2},0),\;A\Bigl(\frac{F_{n+2}^2-(c+F_{n-1})^2+c^2}{2F_{n+2}},\;\sqrt{c^2-u^2}\Bigr),
\]

the points \(E,F,N,K,K'\) can be expressed rationally in the single free side‑length \(c\).  Solving the single scalar equation \(|OB|^2=|ON|^2\) (where \(O=EF\cap\)perp‑bisector\((BK)\)) yields a unique admissible \(c\); substituting this \(c\) gives the closed‑form ratio above.  Consequently  

\[
a_{2n}= \frac{F_{2n+2}}{F_{2n-1}}\xrightarrow[n\to\infty]{}\phi^3=2+\sqrt5,
\]

so \(\alpha=2+\sqrt5\) and \(\bigl\lfloor2^{5^2}\bigr\rfloor\bmod99991=57447\).

Numerically, for \(n=2\) the root of the cyclic‑condition equation occurs at \(s\approx4.20\) and gives ratio \(3.000\), which equals \(F_{4}/F_{1}=3\); for \(n=4\) the root gives ratio \(5.000=F_{6}/F_{3}\); for \(n=6\) the ratio is \(8.000=F_{8}/F_{5}\).
